metadata.title: Construct validity of a mixed-worded mathematics confidence scale: Relations with mathematics achievement in TIMSS 2019

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 Swedish Grade 4 student data (3965 students in 224 classrooms across 145 schools) and explicitly accounts for the nested structure by using Mplus TYPE = COMPLEX with the cluster variable IDCLASS. The authors state that they used the TOT-weight in Mplus to adjust for clustering effects, but they do not report a specific student weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT) in the provided text. Because the analysis is based on structural equation modeling (CFA/ESEM/SEM) rather than ML algorithms, the paper does not discuss applying sampling weights for population-representative estimation beyond the complex-design adjustment. Missingness is handled via FIML and plausible values are incorporated through Mplus imputation, which together affect how the effective sample is used in estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the Swedish Grade 4 sample of TIMSS 2019. The analytic models are based on the nine-item mathematics confidence scale (with alternative operationalisations excluding item 7 or using only positively worded items 1, 4, and 6). Missing item responses were handled using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML), and all five plausible values for mathematics achievement were included via Mplus imputation (TYPE = IMPUTATION).

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Swedish Grade 4 Mathematics confidence scale (9 items; mixed-worded) and Mathematics achievement (PVs)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics confidence construct validity (measurement model fit and factor structure)
main_findings.performance_metrics: CFA Model A1 (inter-item correlations): poor fit (X2=922.840, df=27, RMSEA=.092, CFI=.887, TLI=.850, SRMR=.053). Bifactor ESEM Model A2: good fit (X2=44.449, df=12, RMSEA=.026, CFI=.996, TLI=.988, SRMR=.009). Several items show low factor loadings (<0.40), notably item 7 with problematic loadings (general factor loading -0.29; positive specific factor loading 0.36).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Swedish Grade 4 the study compared multiple measurement operationalisations of the mixed-worded mathematics confidence scale to evaluate construct validity, finding that the bifactor ESEM model (Model A2) achieved the best overall fit while several negatively worded items—especially item 7—showed low/atypical loadings consistent with method effects. This indicates that secondary analyses using the full mixed-worded scale should validate the measurement model and consider excluding or re-operationalising problematic items to avoid biased achievement relationships.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Swedish Grade 4 Mathematics confidence scale (operationalisations B1–B4) and Mathematics achievement (PVs)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics achievement (regressed on latent mathematics confidence operationalisations)
main_findings.performance_metrics: SEM/measurement operationalisations: Model B1 (9 items) standardized coefficient 0.387 (p<.001) with poor fit (χ2(df)=1016.490(35), RMSEA=.084, CFI=.883, TLI=.949, SRMR=.052). Model B2 (8 items excluding item 7) standardized coefficient 0.393 (p<.001) with not acceptable fit (χ2(df)=888.002(27), RMSEA=.090, CFI=.889, TLI=.853, SRMR=.051). Model B3 (3 positively worded items 1,4,6) standardized coefficient 0.322 (p<.001) with good fit (χ2(df)=24.456(2), RMSEA=.053, CFI=.990, TLI=.970, SRMR=.015). Model B4 (target-rotated bifactor ESEM) good fit (χ2/df=70.747/18, CFI=.994, TLI=.984, RMSEA=.027, SRMR=.011) but unexpected factor correlations: G-factor -0.45 (p<.001), negative S-factor 0.10 (p<.001), positive S-factor -0.07 (p=.054).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Swedish Grade 4 the study leveraged alternative operationalisations of the latent mathematics confidence construct to predict mathematics achievement, finding that the most valid and parsimonious operationalisation was Model B3 using only the three positively worded items (significant positive relation with achievement, β=0.322, good fit), while the full mixed-worded/bifactor operationalisation (Model B4) produced counterintuitive achievement associations (e.g., negative G-factor). This indicates that researchers should prefer validated, construct-equivalent item sets (e.g., positively worded subset) when using TIMSS confidence scales in secondary achievement analyses to reduce method-driven distortions.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses Swedish Grade 4 TIMSS 2019 data to evaluate the construct validity of the “student confident in mathematics” mixed-worded scale and to test how different measurement operationalisations relate to mathematics achievement. The mathematics confidence scale comprises nine 4-point Likert items (four positive, five negative), with positively worded items recoded so higher values reflect higher confidence. Mathematics achievement is modeled using TIMSS plausible values (five PVs) within Mplus, and missing item responses are handled with full-information maximum likelihood (FIML). Across four structural equation models, the three-item positively worded operationalisation (items 1, 4, 6) showed good fit (CFI=.990, RMSEA=.053) and a significant positive association with achievement (β=0.322, p<.001). In contrast, the target-rotated bifactor ESEM model fit well (CFI=.994, RMSEA=.027) but yielded counterintuitive factor–achievement relations, suggesting method effects and caution against using the full mixed-worded scale without validation. The paper is cross-sectional, so causal claims are not supported.
